title: Negotiation, closing, pipeline
brief_markdown:
By the time a prospect negotiates, you have already won the argument. Dana does not ask "what can you do on price?" because she doubts Myda; she asks because she is convinced and now wants to feel she got a deal. That is a different conversation from the price objection in Module 7. This chapter is about not giving that value back in the last three minutes, and then keeping twenty deals moving without dropping one.

### Decide what you want before anyone asks
Negotiation runs on five levers: price per unit, quantity, term length, when the money is paid, and renewal. The prospect pulls one; you answer by moving another. So decide now, as a pair, what Myda values most. For a pre-revenue company the order is fixed: cash in the bank first, term length second, everything else is tradeable. Twelve months paid up front beats a higher monthly price paid monthly: an agency that pays monthly can stop in March.

Write the walk-away line down. If the `pricing` artifact says X per month, what is the lowest number you would still sign at, and under which conditions? If it is not written, it will be whatever Dana's tone suggests at minute twelve.

### Retreat one notch, and always trade
Never give something for nothing, and never give two steps when one would close. When Dana says "we're small, can you do something?", the answer is not 20% off. It is "I can do better on the monthly price if we do twelve months paid up front", or "if your three skincare clients come on together". When Marcus says "I only have $1,500 a month", the answer is fewer creators in scope, never the same scope for less. When someone wants three months "to see if it works", the monthly price for three months is two to three times the annual rate; onboarding their creators into Discord is a fixed cost spread over three months instead of twelve.

A 5% concession that gets the order signed today is a good trade. A 30% concession that gets "let me think about it" is the worst outcome available: you paid and got nothing.

### The five asks you will hear
Dana, Marcus and Sofia between them make the same five asks. Decide each answer once, in the Build, and stop improvising on calls.
1. **"We're small, can you do a discount?"** Ask what is behind it (a budget ceiling, someone else's approval, a comparison with another tool) before answering. Then trade.
2. **"Can we get a free month?"** Urgency that is true and cheap: start on the 18th and the rest of the month is free; this price holds until month end; there are three onboarding slots before Christmas. Free time against a signature today is a trade. A free month against nothing is a gift.
3. **"Can we start next quarter?"** The timing objection again. Ask what changes next quarter. Usually nothing; then waiting costs another forty creator videos reviewed on a phone at midnight.
4. **"Can we pilot for free?"** The paid beta at 50% off for a year is the pilot. Free pilots do not get used, because nobody has to justify them to anyone.
5. **"Can we pay on results?"** No, because the result depends on their creators doing the work. Offer a named success metric and a day-30 review instead.

### When you have to say no
Have a backstop. "We agreed as founders that we don't go below X" or "I need to check that with {{founder_2}}" gives Dana a reason to stop pushing that is not personal. Being human works too: the team is small, salaries need paying, and each deal has to be worth its hours. Dana does not give her retainers away either.

If a competitor is in the deal, ask to see the quote, to justify any movement on your side. If you then move, the new pricing comes with one condition: the order form is signed the same day. Otherwise you have entered an auction, and Dana is the auctioneer.

### Run until the money is in the bank
A verbal yes starts a sprint; it does not end the deal. Send the order form while the enthusiasm is warm, within the hour if you can. It holds only what was agreed: scope, price, term, start date, who signs. Legal terms are linked, not attached. Use e-signature, never "print, sign and scan". Make paying easy: a card link costs 3% and saves chasing transfers in three currencies.

Myda is pre-incorporation, and that matters here more than anywhere. What can the founders sign today, who issues the invoice and from which account, and what happens to the agreement when the company is incorporated? The Build settles it, with TODOs for the lawyer or the accountant where it cannot. Then book the kickoff before the signature is dry, and capture the three names Module 9 needs: who signed, who sponsors it, who will use Myda every day.

### Losing well
With a new product in a new category, winning one deal in five is normal and one in three is excellent. So mark deals lost early and honestly. A deal is lost when Dana says so to a direct question, or when the small promises stop being kept: a missed call, a next meeting she will not book, two unanswered emails. Send the breakup email: here is the value we agreed, I do not want to take your time if this is not going to happen, is it not now or not ever? Record the reason (budget, priority, competitor, no real pain, went dark) and a come-back date. Not-now deals return in sixty days as a new opportunity, with whatever engineering shipped as the reason to talk.

### The pipeline
A pipeline is a list of deals, each with a stage that means one exact thing, a next step, and a calendar date for it. The stages are the CRM stages from the `icp` artifact, each with an exit criterion both founders apply the same way: "proposal sent" means Dana asked for pricing, not that you emailed a deck. A deal with no calendared next step is uncovered; the weekly review exists to find those.

Review once a week, together, bottom up: order forms out, verbal yeses without an order form (why?), proposals out, then upwards, biggest deal first within a stage. Anything stuck in a stage for two weeks, or silent for seven days, gets a decision that day: breakup email or closed lost. A stuck deal occupies the slot a live one needs.

The last piece is arithmetic. Revenue goal divided by price is customers. Customers divided by win rate is first conversations. Module 1 asked each of you for a win-rate guess; this module checks it against the CRM log and turns the next two months' revenue goal into LinkedIn notes per week.

### This week
Write the walk-away line and the concession list before the next buyer call. Draft the one-page order form and decide who sends it. Put the weekly pipeline review on both calendars. Close-lost every deal silent for two weeks, with a breakup email and a reason.

**What you build in this module:** the closing playbook and pipeline. Negotiation rules (what is never discounted, which concessions exist and what each is traded for, the walk-away line, who approves an exception), the answers to the five asks, a close-plan template with dates, the order form and payment mechanics for a pre-incorporation company, pipeline stages with exit criteria and the weekly review, and the funnel maths that turns the next two months' revenue goal into weekly activity.

**Drill:** Dana, 15-minute video call after the pilot. She loves it, she wants a discount, a free month and a start after the quarter. Leave with a signed order at list price, or a concession traded for something real, and a date.

build.spec_markdown:
Produce {{company}}'s closing playbook and pipeline, section by section, in this order. Work one question at a time; record each section with update_artifact as soon as it is good enough, then move to the next. Pull the price, unit and term from the `pricing` artifact and the CRM stage names from the `icp` artifact. Do not reopen the price here: if a founder wants to change it, write it under Open questions and move on.

1. **Negotiation rules.** (a) What is never discounted: the per-unit price, the beta terms, the minimum term, or something else; name it. (b) The concession list: every concession {{company}} can give (lower monthly price, remainder of the month free, delayed start, extra creators or brands in scope, extended beta rate) and what each must be traded for: twelve-month term, payment up front, a case study with numbers, an intro to two named agencies or brands, logo on the site, a start date this month. One trade per concession; a concession without a trade is not on the list. (c) The retreat ladder with numbers: list price, first notch, second notch, walk-away line, and the condition attached to each notch. (d) Who approves an exception below the walk-away line (the other founder, within 24 hours, in writing) and where it is recorded.
2. **The five asks.** For each: the question to ask back first, the answer in two or three sentences in Dana's or Marcus's language, and the trade offered. Discount because small; free month; start next quarter; pilot for free; pay on results. Add the competitor-quote rule: ask to see it, move only against a same-day signature.
3. **Close plan template.** A dated table for every deal past verbal yes: verbal yes, order form sent, order form signed, payment received, kickoff call, first feedback delivered to a creator, first result reviewed (day 30). The "what could stop this from happening by then?" question and where its answer is recorded. The three names captured at closing: signer, sponsor, daily user.
4. **Order form and payment mechanics.** What {{company}} can sign today given its legal status (incorporated or not, grant-funded or not): which person or entity signs, what the document is called (order form, beta agreement, letter of intent), and how it transfers on incorporation. The fields of the one-page order form. Where the terms live (linked, not attached). The e-signature tool. Who issues the invoice, from which account, in which currencies (GBP, USD, EUR), card link or bank transfer, and who at {{company}} sends, chases and confirms payment. Anything that needs a lawyer, the tax adviser or a grant contact becomes `TODO: <owner>, <date>`; do not invent legal facts.
5. **Pipeline definition.** Stages using the `icp` CRM stage names; if that artifact does not define them yet, use: Conversation booked, Qualified, Demo done, Proposal sent, Negotiation, Verbal yes, Order form sent, Closed won, Closed lost, Closed unqualified. For each stage: the exit criterion in one sentence both founders would apply the same way, and the maximum days in stage. Required fields per deal: company, persona type (agency or brand), decision maker, sponsor, daily user, value per month, term, stage, next step, next-step date, last-activity date, owner ({{founder_1}} or {{founder_2}}), lost reason, come-back date.
6. **Weekly pipeline review.** Day, time, length, who runs it, where the list lives. Order: bottom of the funnel first, biggest deal first within a stage. The three questions asked of every deal: what is the next step, when is it on the calendar, what could stop it. The lost rules: a direct no; two broken micro-contracts (missed call, meeting not rebooked, two unanswered emails); fourteen days in one stage; seven days silent below Proposal sent. Each triggers a breakup email, then Closed lost with a reason from a fixed list (budget, priority, competitor, no real pain, went dark, wrong person) and a come-back date (sixty days, or the date they named).
7. **Funnel maths.** The revenue goal for the next two months, as a number in the `pricing` unit. Conversion assumptions per step (LinkedIn note sent to reply, reply to first conversation, conversation to demo, demo to proposal, proposal to won), each marked `real` with the count from the CRM log or `guess`. Each founder's Module 1 win-rate guess next to the real number from the CRM log (first conversations logged, deals won). Then the activity required per week to hit the goal: notes per day per founder, conversations per week, demos per week, compared with the current twenty notes a day. Finish with the carrying load: how many open deals each founder can run before next steps start slipping.

Standards to enforce on every section: every rule is a number or a sentence both founders would apply identically; no concession without a trade; nothing legal is invented; the price from the `pricing` artifact is not changed; the funnel maths uses CRM counts wherever they exist and labels every guess. Push back on "it depends" and on concessions that are really discounts in disguise. Mark the artifact done only when both founders agree on the walk-away line and a stranger could run the Dana negotiation from sections 1 and 2 alone.

drill.scenario: Dana's agency has finished the paid beta on three of her skincare clients and her team wants to keep {{company}}. Now she is negotiating, Dana-style: warm, 'love it' every second sentence, and never quite committing. Her list: a discount because 'we're small', a free month, and 'can we start after the quarter'. If you hold the price she will try 'let me think about it'. Your goal: a signed order at the price in the pricing artifact, or a concession traded for something real from the closing playbook (term, payment up front, case study, intro, start date), plus a close plan with dates. Run the call as yourself; she will not hand you the win.
drill.buyer_opening: So the team loved the pilot, honestly, love it. I just need to make the numbers work on my side before I take it to the other partners. What can you do on price?

rows.criterion: Restated the value Dana got from the pilot, in her numbers (hours saved, videos approved), before touching price
Asked what is behind the discount ask (budget ceiling, someone else's approval, a comparison) instead of answering it
Held the list price, or traded each concession for something concrete from the playbook (term, payment up front, case study, intro, start date), one notch at a time
Clarified the decision: who signs, by when, and asked what could stop it
Handled 'after the quarter' and 'let me think about it' with a question or a true reason to start now (rest of month free, onboarding slots, cost of waiting), not pressure
Kept the walk-away line, used the founder backstop when needed, and gave no second concession unprompted
Agreed a close plan with dates: verbal yes, order form, payment, kickoff, first result
Summarised the agreement back, got Dana to confirm it, and named when the order form arrives

rubric.below_threshold_note: Below 10: fix the concession list and the five-asks answers in the closing artifact, then repeat the drill with the same persona when you can; Module 9 is open either way. Carry forward the weakest row as the standing fix; add any ask Dana made that the playbook had no answer for.
